activities.title: Velocity is speed with a direction

differentiation.support: Provide the student notes open at the gradient definition so learners can follow how rise over run on the climbing line gives the speed before they try the worksheet gradient question.

activities.title: Distance-time graphs: the gradient is the speed
Velocity-time graphs: slope is acceleration, area is distance
Out and back: speed without velocity

differentiation.stretch: Ask learners to explain why a flat line at a steady height cannot mean the object has stopped before they take the exit ticket.

activities.title: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose

assessmentPoints: Division answers in the opening activity
Speed and velocity answers in the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can calculate speed as distance over time, such as 100 metres in 20 seconds giving 5 metres per second
I can explain that velocity is speed with a direction, and that a round trip back to the start has zero average velocity
objectives.text: Calculate speed from distance and time, and velocity from displacement and time

assessmentPoints: Gradient answers in the second activity
Graph answers in the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can read the speed off a distance-time graph as rise over run, such as 120 over 60 giving 2 metres per second
I can explain why the gradient of a distance-time graph carries speed units
objectives.text: Read the gradient of a distance-time graph as speed

assessmentPoints: Slope and area answers in the third activity
Trap answers in the fifth activity and the closing exit ticket
successCriteria: I can read acceleration as the slope of a velocity-time graph, such as 20 over 10 giving 2 metres per second squared
I can read the distance travelled as the area under a velocity-time graph, and explain that a flat line means constant velocity, not stopped
objectives.text: Read the gradient of a velocity-time graph as acceleration and the area underneath as distance travelled
